name: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (Ha’il)
summary: A northern Arabian emirate of the Rashidi family based at Ha’il; it defeated the second Saudi state in 1891 and ruled most of central Arabia until Ibn Saud fought back, conquering Ha’il in 1921.

location.value: Northern Najd in the Arabian Peninsula, with Ha’il as capital; it included parts of modern Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Jordan.
location.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

terrain.value: Sandy and rocky desert around the granite Aja and Salma mountains (Jabal Shammar), with scattered oases.

climate.value: Hot desert: very hot summers, cool winters and little, irregular rain.

resources.value: Camels, Arabian horses, date palms and wells in the oases.

disasters.value: Droughts that killed herds; epidemics carried by caravans and pilgrims.

population.value: The article read gives no population estimate for the emirate or for Ha’il.
population.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

urbanisation.value: Ha’il was a walled oasis town with a large mud-brick palace; other settlements were small oasis villages.

disease.value: Smallpox, cholera spread by pilgrims, and eye diseases common in desert towns.

migration.value: Bedouin tribes moved with their herds between seasonal pastures; townsmen traded with Iraq and Syria.

economicBase.value: Camel and horse herding, date farming, and taxes on caravans and pilgrims.

tradeRoutes.value: Ha’il lay on the pilgrim and caravan road from Iraq (Najaf and Baghdad) to Mecca and Medina.

wealth.value: A mixed economy of pastoral nomadism, oasis agriculture, urban crafts and trade; Ha’il was a stop for travellers between Mecca, Medina, Iraq and Iran.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

moneyAndTax.value: Ottoman and other silver coins; the emirs took zakat (religious tax) from tribes and fees from pilgrim caravans.

inequality.value: The Rashidi family and Shammar chiefs above townspeople, lesser tribes and slaves.

governmentType.value: An emirate ruled by the Rashidi family, founded as a vassal of the Second Saudi State.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

keyRulers.value: Abdullah bin Rashid (1836–48). Talal bin Abdullah (1848–68). Muhammad bin Abdullah (1869–97).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Within the Rashidi family, often by murder: several emirs were killed by relatives.

institutions.value: The emir’s court (majlis) at Ha’il, tribal chiefs, and religious judges.

stability.value: Strong under Muhammad bin Rashid (1869–97); after 1906 a series of emirs were murdered within a few years.

eliteConflict.value: Rival branches of the Rashidi family killed each other for power.

armyAndTech.value: Camel- and horse-mounted tribal warriors; rifles and some cannons supplied by the Ottomans.

majorWars.value: Battle of Mulayda (1891); wars with Ibn Saud (1902–21).

territoryChange.value: Took Riyadh after defeating the Saudis and Qasim at Mulayda (1891); lost it to Ibn Saud (1902); conquered in 1921.

alliancesRivals.value: The Rashidis allied with the Ottomans against the Saudis in the 1860s; Ottoman ties grew less profitable as Ottoman influence declined.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

scienceEducation.value: Little formal schooling: Qur’an teaching and some religious scholars at Ha’il.

openness.value: Fairly open: European travellers such as Palgrave (1862), Doughty (1877) and Lady Anne Blunt (1879) visited Ha’il.

communicationTransport.value: Camel caravans across the desert; horses for raiding and war.

religion.value: Sunni Islam; the Rashidis were less strict than the Wahhabi-aligned Saudis.

languageWriting.value: Arabic (Najdi dialects); Bedouin oral poetry was highly valued.

artsArchitecture.value: Mud-brick forts and palaces such as the Barzan palace at Ha’il; Bedouin poetry and horse breeding.

socialStructure.value: The ruling family, Shammar tribal chiefs, Bedouin herders, oasis townspeople and enslaved servants.

sharedIdentity.value: Shammar tribal identity and loyalty to the Rashidi emir.

dailyLife.value: Bedouin lived in tents, moving with camels; townspeople farmed dates. Diets were based on dates, camel milk and bread.

neighbours.value: The Saudis of Riyadh (Najd), the Hejaz, Ottoman Iraq, Kuwait and the Syrian desert.

ideasReligions.value: A less strict Sunni practice than Wahhabism, which became a point of rivalry with the Saudis.

colonisation.value: Never colonised; allied with the Ottomans and sided with them in the First World War.

riseSignals.value: Abdullah bin Rashid was appointed governor of Ha’il in 1836 by Saudi Imam Faisal bin Turki.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: After the victory at Mulayda (1891), when Muhammad bin Rashid ruled most of central Arabia, including Riyadh.

declineSignals.value: Ibn Saud retook Riyadh (1902); Emir Abdulaziz bin Mutaib was killed in battle (1906).

outcome.value: The emirate was ended by the Saudi campaign of late 1921; the article gives surrender on 2 November 1921 (the infobox gives 3 November).
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Emirate of Jabal Shammar (checked 12 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: Main events are well documented; population figures are estimates.
